Understanding test-network
A terminal-first orientation to the files that define a local Fabric sandbox and why each matters for development.

Topic cards
network.sh

organizations/
Holds CA, MSP, user and peer identities for each organization.
configtx & crypto-config
Define how artifacts and cryptographic material are generated.
Visual: relationship
test-network snapshot
A small set of coordinated files and containers that let you run Fabric locally.

You can iterate on chaincode, test channel updates, and learn ordering and identity behavior without a full production setup. The sample network is intentionally self-contained so you can reset and repeat experiments safely.

Control with network.sh

Organizations & MSPs
Where cryptographic identities live and how they map to trust.
Artifacts & generation
configtx and crypto-config control genesis and MSP creation.

When you change configtx.yaml or crypto-config.yaml, regenerate artifacts with the recommended tooling rather than editing generated files inside organizations/. This prevents signature mismatches and broken MSPs.

screens.title: What is test-network and why use it?
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear definition: the test-network folder in fabric-samples is a self-contained local Fabric environment built for rapid setup and experimentation. It includes scripts, Docker Compose descriptors, configuration templates, and sample cryptographic material so you can run peers, orderers, CAs, and optional CouchDB instances without provisioning a separate cluster. Think of it as a local laboratory bench: everything you need for an experiment is available, and you can reset it quickly. A concrete example is bringing up two organizations with peers using a single network. sh invocation — you get running containers, channels, and deployed sample chaincode to exercise endorsement flows. One misconception is to treat the test-network as production-ready; it is not. It simplifies many operational concerns such as certificate lifecycles and persistence. Another useful point: because artifacts are generated from config files, you can change the topology by editing crypto-config. yaml or configtx. yaml and regenerating artifacts, which replaces manual container edits. Key takeaway: use test-network to iterate safely, and always follow a regenerate-then-verify workflow to avoid identity and signature errors. How would you change the number of peers for an organization and verify the new artifacts?

Core Concept › What is test-network
Definition and analogy
A compact, restartable Fabric environment for development and testing. Treat it like a local lab bench where you can run experiments without affecting production.
Why use it
Fast setup, reproducible artifacts, safe experimentation with chaincode and channels.
Concrete example
Run network.sh to start two organizations and deploy sample chaincode to practice endorsement policies.
Common misconception
It is not a production configuration. Security and lifecycle practices are simplified for learning.
Terminal demo snippets
# change into the test-network folder and list contents
cd ~/fabric-dev/fabric-samples/test-network
ls -F
# expected entries: network.sh  docker/  organizations/  scripts/  configtx/  crypto-config.yaml
Key Takeaway

Use the test-network to iterate quickly. Edit the source YAMLs and regenerate artifacts rather than editing generated files.

screens.title: network.sh — the primary control script
screens.narratorSegment: network. sh is the main script you will run to manage the test-network. It wraps multiple Docker Compose calls, environment setup, and Fabric CLI commands into simple subcommands like up, down, createChannel, deployCC and so on. A concrete example: running network. sh up launches the orderer, peers, certificate authorities, and optional CouchDB containers so the network is operational. When you later run a createChannel command, network. sh runs configtxgen-produced transactions and uses peer CLI commands to submit channel creation requests. A common misunderstanding is to try to call Docker Compose directly for every step; while possible, the script ensures the correct environment variables and CLI flags are set consistently. Another practical point: network. sh often calls smaller helper scripts such as deployCC. sh inside scripts/, which encapsulate the chaincode packaging, installation, approval and commit flow. Key takeaway: prefer the scripted path for reproducible results, and inspect network. sh when you need to customize timeouts or logging rather than rewriting sequence logic from scratch. How would you confirm a peer joined a channel after running network. sh createChannel? network.sh — the primary control script means network.sh sequences docker and fabric cli operations so you can reliably bring networks up, create channels, and deploy chaincode.. In practical terms, how network.sh orchestrates bring-up, channels, and chaincode deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process › network.sh walkthrough
What network.sh does
It provides a predictable wrapper for starting and managing the test-network and delegates specialized tasks to helper scripts.
Typical subcommands
  • up — start all containers required by the network
  • down — stop and remove containers and networks
  • createChannel — generate and submit channel creation transactions
  • deployCC — orchestrate packaging, installing and committing chaincode
Helper script example
scripts/deployCC.sh is commonly invoked to perform chaincode lifecycle steps with consistent environment variables and peer contexts.
Terminal code panel
# start the network
./network.sh up

# create a channel
./network.sh createChannel -c mychannel

# deploy example chaincode
./network.sh deployCC -ccn basic -ccp ../asset-transfer-basic/chaincode-go
Key Takeaway

Use network.sh for consistent environment setup and orchestration. Inspect it to customize behavior but avoid duplicating its orchestration logic manually.

screens.title: The docker directory and service definitions
screens.narratorSegment: The docker directory contains the Docker Compose YAML files that define the containers making up the test-network. Files such as docker-compose-test-net. yaml, docker-compose-ca. yaml, and docker-compose-couch. yaml enumerate services like peers, orderers, certificate authorities, and CouchDB instances. Each service block sets the Docker image, ports, volume mounts, and environment variables. A concrete example: changing a peer's port mapping in docker-compose-test-net. yaml will alter how you reach that peer from your host. However, a common pitfall is editing these compose files without considering how network. sh sets environment variables or volumes; network. sh expects certain service names and mounts. If you need to customize topology — for instance, add an extra CouchDB instance — edit the compose files and then use network. sh up so the orchestration script and compose definitions stay in sync. Key takeaway: understand what compose files control and prefer changing topology via the provided config templates and scripts to keep the test-network reproducible. How would you validate a changed service is running after editing compose files? The docker directory and service definitions means they map container images, ports and mounts. keep compose changes coordinated with network.sh to prevent mismatches.. content.html:
Definition › docker directory
Compose file roles
Compose YAMLs declare each service the test-network uses and how they run in Docker.
What is declared
Images, container names, environment, volumes, and ports for peers, orderers, CAs and optional CouchDB.
When to edit
Edit compose files to change container images, add services, or alter volume mounts — but coordinate with network.sh.
Example fragment
# A typical service block
services:
  peer0.org1.example.com:
    container_name: peer0.org1.example.com
    image: hyperledger/fabric-peer:latest
    environment:
      - CORE_PEER_ID=peer0.org1.example.com
Key Takeaway

Compose files are service declarations. Coordinate edits with network.sh so orchestration scripts and compose definitions remain aligned.

screens.title: organizations directory — structure and intent
screens.narratorSegment: The organizations directory mirrors Fabric's permissioned model by storing cryptographic material and MSP definitions per organization. Within organizations you will find peerOrganizations and ordererOrganizations. Peer organizations contain subfolders like ca, msp, peers, and users. The msp subfolder holds CA root certificates, admin certificates, and configuration that peers use to authenticate identities and validate transactions. For ordererOrganizations you will find a similar structure for the ordering service identities and TLS keys. A concrete example: peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/peers/peer0. org1. example. com/tls contains the peer TLS certificates that allow secure gRPC communication. A frequent misconception is thinking these files are mere examples; in the running network they are active credentials. If you change crypto-config. yaml or regenerate certificates, the organizations directory will be replaced — which is why you should never manually edit certs inside organizations/ after generation. Key takeaway: treat organizations/ as a generated, authoritative store of identities that your peers and orderers will actively use at runtime. Comparison › organizations/ hierarchy
Directory hierarchy
Peer and orderer organizations each receive their own directory trees. These mirror identities and service roles used by the network.
peerOrganizations
Contains org folders like org1.example.com with ca, msp, peers, and users subfolders.
ordererOrganizations
Holds ordering service MSPs and orderer node identities under example.com.
Example paths

  • peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/peers/peer0.org1.example.com/tls
  • ordererOrganizations/example.com/msp
Misconception
These files are not decorative; they are live credentials. Manual edits can invalidate signatures and break trust relationships.
Key Takeaway

Treat organizations/ as generated credentials. Change the source YAML and regenerate instead of editing generated certs.

screens.title: peerOrganizations — what you'll find inside
screens.narratorSegment: Dive into peerOrganizations to see the files that make a peer organization operational. Inside each org folder such as org1. example. com you'll typically find ca, msp, users, and peers subdirectories. The ca folder includes the CA certificates used to sign identities. The msp contains the organization's MSP configuration: root CA certificates, intermediate certificates, admin certs, and an MSP config file that defines NodeOUs and other settings. The peers folder contains per-peer identity folders that include TLS certificates and keys used for secure communication and the peer's local MSP. For a concrete example, open peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/peers/peer0. org1. example. com/tls to view the TLS certificate chain the peer presents. One common mistake is copying certificates between organizations to shortcut identity setup — this breaks the trust model because each org must have distinct CA roots. Key takeaway: peerOrganizations is where identity, TLS, and MSP policy files live; keep it consistent by regenerating artifacts from crypto-config. yaml when you need changes. content.html:
Definition › peerOrganizations contents
Common subfolders
  • ca/ — certificate authority artifacts
  • msp/ — MSP root and admin certs and config
  • peers/ — per-peer TLS and identity folders
  • users/ — sample user identities and keystores
Why this matters
Peers and clients validate signatures using the certs in these folders; missing or incorrect certs will prevent transaction endorsement and communication.
Example path and check
ls -F peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/peers/peer0.org1.example.com
# expect: msp/  tls/

ls -F peerOrganizations/org1.example.com/msp
# expect: cacerts/  signcerts/  admincerts/  config.yaml
Key Takeaway

Use simple ls and cat checks to confirm MSP and TLS artifacts exist. Never copy certs between orgs to avoid breaking trust.

screens.title: ordererOrganizations and the genesis block
screens.narratorSegment: Orderer organizations define the ordering service's identity and initial configuration. The ordererOrganizations folder contains the orderer CA, MSP definitions, and orderer node identities. The system genesis block used by the orderer is generated by configtxgen from configtx/configtx. yaml and placed in system-genesis-block. This genesis block contains the initial ordering service configuration, consortium definitions, and policies. A concrete example: when you update configtx. yaml to change the ordering service type or capabilities and then run configtxgen, the resulting genesis block will reflect those changes and the orderer will boot with the new configuration. A common mistake is manually editing the genesis block file inside system-genesis-block; instead, make changes in configtx. yaml and regenerate. screens.title: Common mistakes and safe reset patterns
screens.narratorSegment: A recurring source of failure is manual edits to files inside organizations after cryptogen has created them. Doing so can invalidate certificates and signatures, causing peers and orderers to fail to join channels or validate transactions. A safer pattern is: edit the source YAML (crypto-config. yaml or configtx. yaml), remove the generated directories or backup them, run cryptogen and configtxgen to rebuild artifacts, and then use network. sh down followed by network. sh up to restart the network with the new artifacts. A concrete scenario: if you change the number of peers for org1 in crypto-config. yaml, regenerate artifacts and confirm that new peer0 and peer1 folders appear under peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/peers. Another pitfall is changing Docker Compose service names without updating network. sh expectations — always reconcile compose changes with network. sh. Key takeaway: treat generated artifacts as disposable and always regenerate from source configuration. After a reset, verify certificates exist and that containers start without TLS or identity errors. What checks would you run to confirm the network is healthy post-reset? Process › Common mistakes & reset
Safe reset pattern
  1. Edit source YAML (crypto-config.yaml or configtx.yaml).
  2. Remove or backup generated organizations/ and system-genesis-block/.
  3. Run cryptogen and configtxgen to regenerate artifacts.

Peers fail to join channel with signature or TLS validation errors after manual edits.

Avoid manual edits inside organizations/. Regenerate artifacts from YAML and restart the test-network for a clean, predictable result.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson you will explore the layout and purpose of the test-network folder that ships with fabric-samples. We'll make clear which files you will touch regularly, why they exist, and how they work together when you run the network script. You will see the control script that runs the network, the Docker Compose files that define containers, the organizations folder containing identity material, and the configuration files used to generate channel and genesis artifacts. This matters because working confidently in this sandbox lets you iterate on chaincode and channel configuration without breaking a production system. For example, you will run a simple ls command in the terminal to confirm the presence of network. sh, docker, organizations, configtx, and crypto-config. yaml. A common pitfall is editing generated cryptographic files directly; instead you should update config files and regenerate artifacts. By the end of the chapter you will know where to look to reset, customize, or inspect the test network, and you will be able to answer: which script brings a local test network up and what role do generated MSP folders play?

By the end of this chapter you will reliably locate and explain the main files inside fabric-samples/test-network and use that knowledge to manage a local Fabric sandbox. First, you will identify key directories and files so you know where to look when starting or troubleshooting the network. Second, you will explain the role of network. sh so you can bring the test network up, create channels, and deploy chaincode with confidence. Third, you will describe the organizations directory structure and recognize peer and orderer MSPs and where certificates live. Fourth, you will understand configtx and crypto-config so you can regenerate correct genesis blocks and cryptographic material. Each objective is both practical and diagnostic: being able to list the files is useful, but more important is understanding why altering generated artifacts without regenerating them causes signature failures. As you progress through the lesson cards and terminal walkthroughs, practice the ls and cat commands shown and ask yourself which file you would edit to change the number of peers or to add a new organization. That habit turns knowledge into reliable troubleshooting skill.

This second objectives screen reframes the same four learning goals into practical checkpoints you can use during hands-on work. First, when you list the test-network folder, you should be able to name the files that control orchestration, identity, and artifact generation. For example, identifying network. sh and docker/ means you know where to look to change container behavior. Second, after explaining network. sh, you should be able to run a bring-up and tear-down cycle and interpret common logs. Third, when inspecting organizations/ you should identify where each peer's MSP and certificates reside and explain how those files are used to validate identities. Fourth, for configtx and crypto-config, you will be able to point to the sections you would change to alter channel profiles or the number of peers, and then regenerate artifacts using the supported tools. Each objective closes the loop: change the configuration file, regenerate artifacts, and then verify the organizations directory to avoid manual edits that break signatures.

Start with a clear definition: the test-network folder in fabric-samples is a self-contained local Fabric environment built for rapid setup and experimentation. It includes scripts, Docker Compose descriptors, configuration templates, and sample cryptographic material so you can run peers, orderers, CAs, and optional CouchDB instances without provisioning a separate cluster. Think of it as a local laboratory bench: everything you need for an experiment is available, and you can reset it quickly. A concrete example is bringing up two organizations with peers using a single network. sh invocation — you get running containers, channels, and deployed sample chaincode to exercise endorsement flows. One misconception is to treat the test-network as production-ready; it is not. It simplifies many operational concerns such as certificate lifecycles and persistence. Another useful point: because artifacts are generated from config files, you can change the topology by editing crypto-config. yaml or configtx. yaml and regenerating artifacts, which replaces manual container edits. Key takeaway: use test-network to iterate safely, and always follow a regenerate-then-verify workflow to avoid identity and signature errors. How would you change the number of peers for an organization and verify the new artifacts?

network. sh is the main script you will run to manage the test-network. It wraps multiple Docker Compose calls, environment setup, and Fabric CLI commands into simple subcommands like up, down, createChannel, deployCC and so on. A concrete example: running network. sh up launches the orderer, peers, certificate authorities, and optional CouchDB containers so the network is operational. When you later run a createChannel command, network. sh runs configtxgen-produced transactions and uses peer CLI commands to submit channel creation requests. A common misunderstanding is to try to call Docker Compose directly for every step; while possible, the script ensures the correct environment variables and CLI flags are set consistently. Another practical point: network. sh often calls smaller helper scripts such as deployCC. sh inside scripts/, which encapsulate the chaincode packaging, installation, approval and commit flow. Key takeaway: prefer the scripted path for reproducible results, and inspect network. sh when you need to customize timeouts or logging rather than rewriting sequence logic from scratch. How would you confirm a peer joined a channel after running network. sh createChannel? network.sh — the primary control script means network.sh sequences docker and fabric cli operations so you can reliably bring networks up, create channels, and deploy chaincode.. In practical terms, how network.sh orchestrates bring-up, channels, and chaincode deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The docker directory contains the Docker Compose YAML files that define the containers making up the test-network. Files such as docker-compose-test-net. yaml, docker-compose-ca. yaml, and docker-compose-couch. yaml enumerate services like peers, orderers, certificate authorities, and CouchDB instances. Each service block sets the Docker image, ports, volume mounts, and environment variables. A concrete example: changing a peer's port mapping in docker-compose-test-net. yaml will alter how you reach that peer from your host. However, a common pitfall is editing these compose files without considering how network. sh sets environment variables or volumes; network. sh expects certain service names and mounts. If you need to customize topology — for instance, add an extra CouchDB instance — edit the compose files and then use network. sh up so the orchestration script and compose definitions stay in sync. Key takeaway: understand what compose files control and prefer changing topology via the provided config templates and scripts to keep the test-network reproducible. How would you validate a changed service is running after editing compose files? The docker directory and service definitions means they map container images, ports and mounts. keep compose changes coordinated with network.sh to prevent mismatches.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The organizations directory mirrors Fabric's permissioned model by storing cryptographic material and MSP definitions per organization. Within organizations you will find peerOrganizations and ordererOrganizations. Peer organizations contain subfolders like ca, msp, peers, and users. The msp subfolder holds CA root certificates, admin certificates, and configuration that peers use to authenticate identities and validate transactions. For ordererOrganizations you will find a similar structure for the ordering service identities and TLS keys. A concrete example: peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/peers/peer0. org1. example. com/tls contains the peer TLS certificates that allow secure gRPC communication. A frequent misconception is thinking these files are mere examples; in the running network they are active credentials. If you change crypto-config. yaml or regenerate certificates, the organizations directory will be replaced — which is why you should never manually edit certs inside organizations/ after generation. Key takeaway: treat organizations/ as a generated, authoritative store of identities that your peers and orderers will actively use at runtime. How would you confirm that the TLS cert for a peer matches what the peer is currently serving? organizations directory — structure and intent means each organization's msp and certificates live here; they are active credentials used by peers and orderers at runtime.. In practical terms, how peerorganizations and ordererorganizations map identities and trust. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Dive into peerOrganizations to see the files that make a peer organization operational. Inside each org folder such as org1. example. com you'll typically find ca, msp, users, and peers subdirectories. The ca folder includes the CA certificates used to sign identities. The msp contains the organization's MSP configuration: root CA certificates, intermediate certificates, admin certs, and an MSP config file that defines NodeOUs and other settings. The peers folder contains per-peer identity folders that include TLS certificates and keys used for secure communication and the peer's local MSP. For a concrete example, open peerOrganizations/org1. example. com/peers/peer0. org1. example. com/tls to view the TLS certificate chain the peer presents. One common mistake is copying certificates between organizations to shortcut identity setup — this breaks the trust model because each org must have distinct CA roots. Key takeaway: peerOrganizations is where identity, TLS, and MSP policy files live; keep it consistent by regenerating artifacts from crypto-config. yaml when you need changes. How would you check that a peer's MSP includes the expected admin certificate? peerOrganizations — what you'll find inside means contains ca artifacts, msp definitions, per-peer tls keys, and user identities that together define a peer organization's trust.. In practical terms, files every peer organization contains and their roles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Orderer organizations define the ordering service's identity and initial configuration. The ordererOrganizations folder contains the orderer CA, MSP definitions, and orderer node identities. The system genesis block used by the orderer is generated by configtxgen from configtx/configtx. yaml and placed in system-genesis-block. This genesis block contains the initial ordering service configuration, consortium definitions, and policies. A concrete example: when you update configtx. yaml to change the ordering service type or capabilities and then run configtxgen, the resulting genesis block will reflect those changes and the orderer will boot with the new configuration.
